FinanceTab.title: Speed camera fault may have allowed drivers to escape fines
FinanceTab.text:
Further problems with the accuracy of speed cameras on English roads have been uncovered which may have allowed drivers to slip through the cracks and escape fines.

National Highways discovered issues with speed cameras last year, affecting 154 out of 400 cameras but, following an investigation, said it had found another fault on units monitoring roads including those running between Huntingdon and Cambridge.

The Home Office has revoked approval that allows footage from the cameras to be used as evidence in legal proceedings. US firm Verra Mobility operates the cameras but National Highways said it will now end the contract.

Roads minister Justin Madders said: "We can't take chances with this.

"If we're going to prosecute people, we need to be confident the system is working as it should. That's why we've taken the action we have."

In a statement, Verra Mobility said it "remains fully committed to delivering reliable, innovative technology that helps make roads safer".

The fault affected all of the variable speed cameras on smart motorways, and a section of the A14 between Huntingdon and Cambridge as well as the A1 approach junction to the A14.

A spokesperson for National Highways said that Verra's camera system had been selected on the basis that it maintained Home Office approval.

The agency said that since that was no longer the case "we are ending our contractual relationship to use the cameras for enforcement".

It added: "We are considering all further commercial and legal options that may be appropriate."

The BBC has contacted Verra Mobility for comment.

Madders said that the enforcement of speed limits continues to be conducted through a range of different tactics, including mobile cameras as well as marked and unmarked police patrols.

But he admitted that the camera system will not be fully fixed until sometime next year.

Rod Dennis, senior policy officer at the RAC motoring organisation, said: "Malfunctioning speed cameras on smart motorways do more than just let speeding drivers get away with breaking the law and endangering lives – they further undermine confidence in the very types of road we know drivers already have serious misgivings about."

There are 4,000 cameras across the entire road network.

In December 2025, National Highways, which runs England's motorways, blamed an "anomaly" in how variable speed cameras were interacting with speed limit signs on some A roads and motorways.

For example, on a road where the speed limit increases, a driver may see a sign showing 60mph but the camera recording it may still be working on the basis of a previous 40mph speed limit.

The fault led to 2,650 wrongful speed camera activations between 2021 and the end of last year.

Those who had been wrongfully fined have been reimbursed.

As National Highways continued to test the system, it discovered a further problem "relating to how some of these cameras may activate in specific and rare circumstances".

It said that according to its calculations, "the circumstances in which the latest issue could occur are extremely rare, and there is no evidence to suggest it has impacted enforcement".

Nevertheless, it said it was "taking immediate steps to ensure compliance is maintained at relevant locations".

It said it would out further traffic officer patrols in place to monitor the sites.

FinanceTab.title: We were priced out of the market, so we bought a home with strangers
FinanceTab.text:
When Elizabeth and Tom Wilcox realised they could never afford to buy the home they wanted for themselves and their two children, they decided to take a leap of faith.

They'd find another couple with young kids, complete strangers to them, and propose that they go halves on a property and all move in together.

Based in Vancouver, which has long had some of the highest house prices in Canada, the Wilcoxes were desperate to buy a home that had a back garden for their children to play in.

"We wanted a house with a yard that could fit a trampoline, in a walkable neighbourhood, but we couldn't afford it," says Elizabeth, a project manager in the healthcare sector.

With a budget of C$1m ($700,000; £500,000) all they could hope for was a small apartment with a balcony at best.

That was when Elizabeth came up with the idea of buying with another family.

They placed an advert in a local estate agent's e-newsletter, but it took two years before they finally met a family whom they clicked with – Ashley Pullman and her husband and two children.

In 2023, the Wilcoxes and the Pullmans co-bought a six-bedroom, detached house, complete with a back garden, for C$1.85m.

The two families split the deposit of C$250,000, and continue to go halves on the monthly mortgage payments of C$3,900. They also divide bills and other expenses equally, such as any necessary home repairs.

Elizabeth says the arrangement has saved both families "tens of thousands of dollars".

While there is no official data available for the number of people buying homes with people they previously didn't know, Parimal Gosai says he has seen a big increase in interest in Toronto as a response to high property prices.

Gosai is the founder and CEO of Husmates, an app and website that connects people in Canada's largest city who are looking to potentially buy a home with a stranger.

It can be seen as "a financial relationship, and that takes emotions out of it", he says.

It's unclear how common this phenomenon is elsewhere in the world. David Hollingworth, from British mortgage broker L&C, says while he hasn't come across it himself, he thinks it also happens in the UK, though is "very niche".

"I remember that before Covid-19 there was a matchmaking event in a London pub, like speed dating, for people looking to buy a house with a stranger," he says. "How successful this was I don' t know."

Three years on, the Wilcoxes and the Pullmans say their living arrangement is still working out.

While each family has some private living spaces, such as their own kitchens, they share the big basement-level living room, which includes a home gym in one corner, and a shared freezer.

"If someone says they're in the basement to work out, we know not to go there for a bit, and it's never been an issue," says Elizabeth.

Ashley agrees that there are no problems. "Maybe it's arrogance but my husband and I felt like we were the type of people who could live with strangers," she says.

In the case of both Sabrina's house in Toronto and the Wilcox and Pullman property in Vancouver, they have legal agreements in place in case someone wants to sell up and move out.

For both homes, reasonable notice periods are specified, and for Sabrina's, the departing housemate is required to give those remaining the first opportunity to buy their share.

Toronto real estate lawyer Tanya Walker says such legal assurances are vital. "You need something legally binding instead of a bunch of emails and Facebook messages that can be too messy to collect if a dispute comes up," Walker says.

Back in Vancouver, Elizabeth says that neither family has a timeframe for how long they will live in the house. "All of us are really happy with the set-up and location so it would be hard to move.

"I can't put a price on how it felt to watch the kids jump on the trampoline for the first time, or run in circles on our patch of green grass."

FinanceTab.title: Create more jobs for under-25s by cutting National Insurance, key report urges
FinanceTab.text:
National Insurance (NI) paid by firms on under-25s should be gradually lowered to help create more jobs, a major report will urge.

There are nearly one million 16-24 year-olds not in employment, education or training (Neets) in the UK, official figures show.

Reducing NI costs for firms starting with retail and hospitality firms - which provide almost 40% of jobs for these people - will help improve their opportunities, the report will suggest.

Collette Osborne, a hairdresser who owns two salons in Nottingham, said she feels "suffocated by employment costs" including NI and while she used to employ eight apprentices a year, now she cannot afford to take on any.

Her workforce has more than halved to 21 staff. Osborne told the BBC it costs "around £60,000 to train an apprentice before we can actually start allowing them onto customers' heads".

She said she has had parents so desperate for their children to find employment at her salons that some have even offered to pay their wages.

"I'm inundated with applications - and I mean inundated - which is heartbreaking because I can't take them on," she said.

Osborne does not feel she is getting help to offer jobs to youngsters.

"I feel like the government's foot is firmly on my neck," she said. "They promise breathing space. I feel suffocated, suffocated by employment costs."

The independent report by former Labour minister Alan Milburn has been in the works for a year and will be published on Tuesday in full.

He has already unveiled some of his proposals including:

Reducing benefits - under-25s should no longer be able to claim the health element of UK-wide Universal Credit or personal independence payment (Pip), which is the main disability benefit in England and Wales

A legal guarantee of a job, training or employment support with those who refuse to take up potentially losing their benefits.

Doubling the threshold at which businesses start paying NI for 21 to 24-year-olds from £5,000 to £10,000.

At the moment, businesses pay no employer NI contributions for workers younger than 21 or for apprentices under 25 – unless they earn above a threshold of £50,270.

However, for non-apprentices aged 21-24, employers pay 15% on annual earnings above £5,000.

This has been the situation since April 2025, after the then Chancellor Rachel Reeves increased the rate from 13.8% and lowered the threshold from £9,100.

Under Sir Keir Starmer, the government raised NI for firms but Milburn will say the Neets issue was not started by the increase.

Immediately axing NI for 21 to 24-year-olds would cost £5.1bn, according to research by the Resolution Foundation, a left-leaning think tank.

Milburn is set to say that an immediate across-the-board cut in employer NI is not the best use of several billions of pounds of public money.

But shadow work and pensions secretary, Helen Whately, said the government should "just stop doing the taxing".

FinanceTab.title: Bryson DeChambeau joins DP World Tour following LIV Golf collapse
FinanceTab.text:
Two-time US Open champion Bryson DeChambeau has agreed to join the DP World Tour for next season.

DeChambeau was among a host of star names who joined LIV Golf four years ago and maintained his commitment even after Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund withdrew its financial backing for the breakaway tour in April.

Earlier this month the 33-year-old American said he "gave everything" to keep LIV Golf alive as the tour confirmed its intention to wind down operations.

As first reported in the Telegraph,, external DeChambeau successfully submitted his application to join the European Tour before Sunday's deadline.

DeChambeau has already confirmed he will compete in Gary Player's Nedbank Golf Challenge - a DP World Tour event - in South Africa in December.

As a recent major champion DeChambeau has been given 'category one' membership by the DP World Tour, which means he is guaranteed entry to any event across the season.

Dustin Johnson, Cameron Smith and Bubba Watson - other former major champions who defected to LIV - have signed agreements to receive invitations to a specific number of tournaments.

Veteran English trio Ian Poulter, Lee Westwood and Paul Casey, plus Northern Ireland's Graeme McDowell, are among a number of ex-LIV players who are eligible to play on the DP World Tour in 2027.

The full-time return of Spain's Jon Rahm and England's Tyrrell Hatton, who did not resign their memberships, has also been confirmed.

"There has been significant change in the landscape of men's professional golf over the past 12 months," said DP World Tour chief executive Guy Kinnings.

"As golf's global tour, we have taken a pragmatic approach to this unique and unprecedented situation as we go into next year, always with the best interests of our entire membership at the forefront of our minds."

As one of the poster boys of LIV Golf, and one of the biggest names in the sport, it was intriguing to see what DeChambeau would do next.

With LIV golfers automatically banned for a year by the PGA Tour, it was thought he might decide to focus on his YouTube and social media channels - which have attracted a new, younger audience of many millions - over the next 12 months.

But joining the DP World Tour is a logical option for the big-hitting American, who reportedly received £95m, external to join LIV in 2022 and earned almost £50m in prize money over four seasons.

Signing up for the European-based tour means he can play the traditional format of the game on a regular basis and offers a pathway back to the PGA Tour.

The leading 10 players on the DP World Tour in a season are guaranteed PGA Tour cards for the following season, which was a route taken by Patrick Reed - DeChambeau's former US Ryder Cup team-mate - when he left LIV before the start of the 2026 season.

For the DP World Tour, DeChambeau brings further star power to their product.

DeChambeau will join the likes of European superstars Rory McIlroy and Tommy Fleetwood as full-time members, and boosts the tour's stock as the golfing landscape continues to realign following LIV's demise.

"I think a name like Bryson DeChambeau and everything he brings with him, good and bad, he brings eyeballs, which is a good thing for tournaments," McIlroy said earlier this month.

Six-time major champion McIlroy also claimed those connected to LIV were expressing an ambition to "destroy the European Tour" during this year's Masters.

Instead, the Saudi-backed venture is to be liquidated and has led to an influx of big-names joining the DP World Tour.

As well as DeChambeau being given membership for the first time, it was announced that Johnson, Smith and Watson are among a group of nine former LIV players allowed to play a limited number of events.

They will be picked at the discretion of the DP World Tour to "add value to those tournaments", which is designed to prevent full-time members from missing playing opportunities.

On allowing former LIV players to join the tour, Kinnings added: "We realise there are different viewpoints.

"But this approach, discussed and agreed with our tournament committee and allied to this responsibly managed programme of invites, will add value which, in turn, will benefit the tour as a whole."

FinanceTab.title: Live Updates: Nvidia to Release First Earnings Report Since Leadership Turmoil
FinanceTab.text:
Other rival chipmakers also fell. Advanced Micro Devices and Micron Technology both dropped over 3 percent. The Philadelphia Semiconductor index, a benchmark for the industry, dropped 1.6 percent.

Nvidia’s slide might seem peculiar given that the company, by almost any measure, is expected to report staggering growth later on Tuesday, when it reports earnings for the three months through October 25. But for investors watching the results, their concern is more with what Nvidia is likely to do going forward, and less about the astronomical growth it has already produced.

The worry across the A.I. industry is that a mix of supply-chain bottlenecks, the potential for new regulation and the industry’s increasing dependence on debt could slow future growth. With Nvidia’s leadership crisis, those questions are even more pertinent, and investors will be looking to see if Nvidia expects to be able to maintain its current trajectory, or whether it forecasts a slowdown.

Since its peak in October, Nvidia has lost a third, or roughly $2 trillion, of its market value. And it is on course for a decline of roughly 17 percent for the year, its first annual drop since 2022.

Mr. Huang resigned from the company he co-founded after he admitted he was unfaithful to his wife. The New York Times has reported that he had an affair with an employee at Nvidia, as well as a businesswoman who U.S. intelligence has determined is an asset for Chinese intelligence.

Mr. Huang has the backing of a number of allies in Silicon Valley and Wall Street. But Nvidia’s board is not considering reinstating him, according to a person familiar with their thinking who spoke on condition of anonymity.

The board, which includes early investors and business partners who have been close to Mr. Huang for decades, said on Tuesday it had formed a committee to oversee Nvidia’s national security policies, compliance with U.S. trade restrictions and risk management for global trade.

Mr. Huang’s allies started a campaign for his return to Nvidia over the weekend, saying his exit from the company would set the United States back in the artificial intelligence race and blaming Nvidia’s board for bowing to pressure. President Trump also said on Monday that he “would not mind” if Mr. Huang returned to his job and that he thought Mr. Huang had “learned a big lesson.”

The pressure campaign is one of several significant challenges for Nvidia’s board and its interim chief executive, Colette Kress, Nvidia’s longtime chief financial officer who stepped in last week to lead the company.

Nvidia is expected to report strong quarterly earnings on Tuesday afternoon. Its stock price was down as much as 3 percent in midday trading on Tuesday, continuing a weekslong slide that has cut nearly $2 trillion in the total value of the company.

Rethinking how Nvidia — which is still one of the most valuable companies in the world — is run will also be difficult. Mr. Huang led the company with an executive team of more than 60 people, many of whom are longtime loyalists. And members of his family, including his children, Madison and Spencer, and his son-in-law, Nico Caprez, remain in prominent positions at the company.

After Mr. Huang’s affair with the Chinese intelligence asset became public, Nvidia’s board started an investigation led by its independent board members. His affair with an Nvidia employee emerged days after. The board met in an emergency meeting that day and Mr. Huang resigned the following morning.

“I have made serious mistakes in my personal life,” Mr. Huang said on Tuesday. “I created problems for the board that I deeply regret.”

His statement was received with skepticism by some in Washington.

Representative Hakeem Jeffries, Democrat of New York and a front-runner to be the next speaker of the House, said on Tuesday that Mr. Huang should not return as Nvidia’s chief executive, pointing to concerns that China has been gaining access to Nvidia’s advanced A.I. chips by using data center outside China’s borders.

“The highest rungs of American technology potentially being diverted to the Chinese Communist Party in ways that put Americans potentially at risk — that’s all unacceptable,” Mr. Jeffries said.

“Slow your roll there,” Senator Ruben Gallego, Democrat of Arizona, said in a social media post responding to Mr. Huang’s statement. “You have to answer some questions first.”

Have you worked with Nvidia? We want to hear from you.

The strategy has drawn billions of dollars in investment to the region. But in Washington, officials seeking tighter controls on China’s A.I. sector have increasingly viewed data centers as a workaround that poses economic and national security risks.

Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, was ousted last week after revelations he had an affair with a woman who formed a Singaporean data center company called Megaspeed. U.S. authorities deemed the woman, Alice Huang, to be an asset for Chinese intelligence services, and they are investigating Megaspeed over allegations of smuggling chips to China. China has denied that Ms. Huang was spying for it.

Separately, Nvidia’s board of directors announced on Tuesday that it had established a committee to oversee “the company’s national security policies, export control compliance and global trade risk management.” Nvidia’s board is engaged in a search for a permanent successor to Mr. Huang. The company’s interim chief executive, Colette Kress, is set to preside over the release of the company’s latest quarterly financial results later on Tuesday.

Shares of technology companies tumbled on Tuesday. In trading in Hong Kong, Alibaba fell more than 5 percent, while Tencent’s stock dropped nearly 4 percent. The Chinese A.I. firms MiniMax Group fell more than 7 percent and Z.AI declined more than 5 percent. In the United States, tech stocks slid lower, pulling the Nasdaq index down more than 1 percent. Nvidia shares faced choppy trading ahead of its earnings results, which are expected after the market closes.

Governments across Southeast Asia were scrambling to assess the administration’s 132-page policy, released by the Commerce Department on Monday, as President Trump traveled to Asia for diplomatic meetings.

The timing illustrated how A.I. has moved to the center of global diplomacy. Mr. Trump was expected to meet leaders of several affected countries at the ASEAN summit of 11 Southeast Asian nations in Manila. Then, he traveled to Shenzhen, China, for the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation, or APEC, forum.

The rules, which take effect in 90 days, will require overseas data center operators to obtain a license from the United States government before supplying a “significant volume” of computing power to companies based in countries deemed high-risk, including China, Iran and Russia.

Licenses would also be required to export advanced chips to companies headquartered in Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, Indonesia or Brazil, countries the Trump administration identified as posing a heightened smuggling risk.

The Singaporean government said in a statement on Tuesday that it was investigating Megaspeed and was “engaging the relevant U.S. authorities on the scope and implementation of the measure.”

“As a global hub for technology and trade, Singapore will continue to safeguard the integrity of our business environment and continued access to advanced semiconductors and computing capabilities for legitimate companies operating here, and act against those who flout our laws,” the statement read.

Indonesia said it was seeking industry input and pledged to enforce American export controls. The government is developing a trade framework to “facilitate legitimate trade” while preventing sensitive technologies from being “diverted or misused,” the country’s Government Communication Agency said.

Steve Okun, chief executive of APAC Advisors, a geopolitical consulting firm, said countries such as Malaysia had benefited from maintaining close ties with Washington and Beijing. The new restrictions could make that balancing act harder to sustain.

“The ‘don’t make us choose’ era is coming to an end,” he said. “When it comes to A.I. and sensitive technologies, countries will need to choose the U.S.-led tech stack versus China.”

Ong Kian Ming, Malaysia’s former deputy minister for investment, trade and industry, said he hoped the Trump administration, which has been divided over A.I. chip export restrictions, would revise the rules before they take effect.

Otherwise, he said, the restrictions could create an opening for Chinese companies to offer competing chips. “This may mitigate some of the negative impact of not allowing these players to access Nvidia GPU chips,” he said.

Xinyun Wu and Aruni Soni contributed reporting.

Nvidia exports have exposed a rift in the Trump administration between officials who believe American A.I. technology needs to be kept out of China for national security reasons and others who want a more hands-off approach to export controls.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a TV interview on Friday that his department had been pushing for months to add Megaspeed to a trade blacklist, but that the Commerce Department “holds the pen.”

“You will have to ask them about their internal processes,” he said.

That the Justice Department was included in the Monday night announcement appeared to add heft to the investigation’s importance and signaled to critics that administration officials did not intend to ignore the issue.

Megaspeed was created and led for a time by Alice Huang, who U.S. officials say was an asset for Chinese intelligence. The New York Times reported last year that she and Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, had a close relationship, and last week Mr. Huang admitted that he had been unfaithful to his wife with Ms. Huang.

Mr. Huang resigned from Nvidia last week following another revelation that he had had a relationship with a woman who worked for him. It was a stunning downfall for an executive who led a firm that for a time was the most valuable publicly traded company in the world.

Megaspeed has said that it complies with all laws and that Ms. Huang currently has no role in the company. She has not returned requests for comment, and the Chinese government has dismissed the spying claims.

The Monday night news release confirming the criminal investigation was also unusual because officials do not typically discuss their inquiries until they are completed. The departments said that they would work together to “bring the full extent of the law against Megaspeed for any criminal conduct that may have occurred.”

President Trump on Monday acknowledged that Mr. Bessent and Mr. Lutnick had been at odds over how hard to crack down on a loophole that has allowed China to access advanced A.I. chips through data centers in other countries.

“One wants to be friendly with China, and one wants to have a blowup with China,” Mr. Trump said of his two cabinet secretaries. “Both are acceptable, but they’re different views.”

The news release said that the Commerce Department had initiated an investigation into Megaspeed in 2024 for potential export control violations. In May 2025, the department requested records from Nvidia on its sales to Megaspeed. Commerce officials visited the company in June 2025 and interviewed Ms. Huang, it said.

The Justice Department then took the lead role in the Megaspeed criminal investigation, the news release said.

The New York Times reported last week that the Commerce Department investigation was halted last fall under atypical circumstances, after department investigators received an email from Nvidia’s general counsel seeking information about the inquiry.

Nvidia’s general counsel said that a top official at the department had given him permission to reach out about the case, alarming others in the department. The incident raised questions about what Commerce officials had discussed with Nvidia, and some viewed the interaction as potentially tainting the case. It was then transferred to the Justice Department.

The Commerce Department also said that Nvidia had placed Megaspeed on its “no-sell” list in June 2025.

But trade records obtained by The Times from ImportGenius, a data platform, show that Speedmatrix, a Megaspeed subsidiary in Malaysia, continued receiving large shipments of Nvidia technology for eight months after that.

Between October 2026 and February 2026, Speedmatrix received shipments of more than $800 million of export-controlled Nvidia A.I. technology, including Blackwell and H200 chips, which were banned from being sent to China.

Most of the Speedmatrix shipments went through third-party manufacturers that buy chips from Nvidia and make them into servers. But in February 2026, trade records show that Nvidia International Inc. sent a $13 million shipment of electronic equipment to Speedmatrix.

Nvidia provided a similar statement to The Times about the “block list” last week. It said that it received permission from the Commerce Department to ship some repair parts to Megaspeed after imposing its “block.”

Nvidia continues to list Megaspeed on its website as a cloud partner. Megaspeed advertised the relationship as recently as October, calling its Indonesian unit “a premier business partner of Nvidia.”

The Commerce Department said it had charged 17 defendants across six separate investigations over allegations of smuggling and sharply increased monetary penalties compared with those in the Biden administration.

Mr. Lutnick has clashed in recent months with other senior officials over rules that would clamp down on data centers in Southeast Asia that serve Chinese clients. The Commerce Department issued that rule Monday, but took the unusual step of saying that it had been “written by and at the direction of the Department of Treasury and the National Security Council,” both agencies it had clashed with.

In a note to Nvidia’s employees, Ms. Kress said she believed “deeply in this company” and called its employees “our greatest strength.” She said Nvidia would have a companywide meeting on Nov. 18 to discuss its future.

She will remain Nvidia’s chief financial officer while serving as its interim chief executive officer until the board names a permanent successor. The board said on Thursday that it had started a search for that replacement and would consider internal and external candidates. Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Ms. Kress, who joined Nvidia in 2013, is leading the company as it enters an uncertain next chapter. Under the leadership of Mr. Huang, Nvidia grew from a niche maker of computer chips used for video games to one of the most valuable public companies in the world and the linchpin of the artificial intelligence boom. Nvidia controls an estimated 90 percent of the market for the chips used in the big A.I. projects that are driving the U.S. economy.

Ms. Kress, 59, faces a challenging road. She is temporarily taking over a company that has been tightly controlled by her predecessor. Mr. Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and had managed all aspects of its business with a flat structure that placed him at the center of its day-to-day operations.

His family members had steadily risen through its ranks in recent years. And while Ms. Kress is already familiar to Wall Street, she does not have Mr. Huang’s relationships with Nvidia’s sprawling supply chain or Washington.

Ms. Kress has a bachelor’s degree in finance from the University of Arizona and a master’s degree in business administration from Southern Methodist University. She previously worked in finance at Texas Instruments, Microsoft and Cisco, before joining Nvidia in 2013.

Mr. Huang interviewed 22 candidates before hiring Ms. Kress as chief financial officer. At the time, Ms. Kress’s young sons, who were avid gamers, encouraged her to join Nvidia. During her first week on the job, Ms. Kress asked Mr. Huang how long he thought he would want her in the role.

“I said, ‘For as long as we shall live and death do us part,’” Mr. Huang said on a podcast this year.

As chief financial officer, Ms. Kress was responsible for communicating with Nvidia’s investors and Wall Street. Over the past four years, Ms. Kress delivered a rosy message on quarterly earnings calls as Nvidia’s revenue and profits soared, though she also expressed concerns about the financial impact of American policies that restrict the sale of advanced chips to China.

In 2013, Nvidia’s revenue was $4.28 billion. Its revenue in its most recent fiscal year was more than 50 times that, at nearly $215.94 billion. In August, Ms. Kress told analysts and investors that Nvidia expects to grow 70 percent next year.

Ms. Kress has benefited from Nvidia’s skyrocketing stock price in recent years. As of March, she owned more than 4.4 million shares in the company, according to its most recent annual report, a stake that was worth about $780.4 million at the time. That makes Ms. Kress one of the largest individual shareholders of Nvidia. Its largest individual shareholder, with a 3.56 percent stake, is Mr. Huang.

Ms. Kress’s transition — as well as that of the permanent successor to Mr. Huang — could be complicated by how Mr. Huang managed Nvidia. He led the company with an executive team of more than 60 people who directly reported to him, many of whom are longtime loyalists. That flat structure will be difficult to unwind. On a podcast in January, Mr. Huang described his executive team as a group of “60 people who could be world-class C.E.O.s for many other companies.”

For the time being, Ms. Kress will be C.E.O. for Nvidia.

FinanceTab.title: Deutsche Bank dismissed warnings about dealings with risky clients, reports claim
FinanceTab.text:
Deutsche Bank reportedly dismissed warnings about its dealings with risky clients, including high-profile Russian oligarchs, to protect profits, the findings of an investigation into a trove of leaked bank documents indicate.

A leak of 15m internal files is reported to show that the troubled German bank repeatedly ignored concerns by its compliance officers about its risk-taking, despite having already been caught being used to launder billions of dollars for Russian criminals, spies and oligarchs between 2010 and 2015.

The investigations, which were published by media outlets including Der Spiegel, the Financial Times, the New York Times and Le Monde, will represent a fresh blow for Deutsche Bank, which has struggled to repair its reputation after a number of scandals and dealings with controversial clients including the US president, Donald Trump, and the sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

Deutsche Bank said on Tuesday that the issues raised in the investigations “date back many years, in some cases as much as two decades” and had been addressed by its leadership. “Where relevant, we reviewed these matters at the time and worked closely with regulators.”

However, the reports suggested Deutsche Bank prioritised profit ahead of internal controls, and continued to expand its Russian business until 2021, despite warnings from internal compliance officers and growing geopolitical tensions between Nato allies and Moscow.

Deutsche Bank allegedly resisted pulling out of Russia even after the Kremlin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, before the bank did a U-turn and exiting the country in March that year.

The investigations suggested Deutsche Bank was driven by competitive pressure, including from American banks, and that its chief executive, Christian Sewing, pursued a growth strategy that involved doing business with a list of customers known as its “most sensitive clients”. That covered roughly 50 corporate clients ranked by how close they were to the Kremlin, and other potential risks including financial crime, according to the Financial Times.

Some names allegedly on that list included: Russia’s state-owned gas company Gazprom; petrochemicals group Sibur; and oligarchs including the aluminium magnate Oleg Deripaska, the report said.

Outside its Russian dealings, the German lender is facing fresh scrutiny for allegedly processing almost $600m (£454m) of suspicious payments linked to Epstein, much higher than previously known. Deutsche said it “regrets [its] historical relationship” with Epstein and that it had made “considerable investments in strengthening controls”.

The lender is also accused of accidentally leaking Trump’s tax documents to another client during his first term in office, which Deutsche Bank allegedly kept secret from the White House. Deutsche Bank said it did not comment on former or existing client relationships. Deutsche Bank cut ties with Trump in 2021.

The reports prompted a 4% drop in Deutsche Bank’s German-listed shares on Tuesday.

Deutsche Bank issued a public statement in response to the investigation on Tuesday, saying it had “gone through a fundamental transformation” under Sewing.

“We made substantial investments in our control environment while restoring sustainable profitability, as evidenced by record profits in 2025 as well as in recent quarters. This involved €7bn of direct investments in our control environment between 2019 and 2025.”

The bank added: “We remain committed to ensuring continuous enhancements of our control environment and a culture of integrity and completing any outstanding remediation.”

“Regardless of how the information was obtained, it includes confidential information about clients, employees and other third parties, which remains legally protected. We have acted, and will continue to act, decisively to protect this,” the bank said.

FinanceTab.title: Markets drop ahead of Nvidia’s results; Jensen Huang says he’d be ‘honoured’ to return as CEO – as it happened
FinanceTab.text:
Jensen Huang has thrown his hat into the ring to return to his role running Nvidia, less than a week after being ousted amid an alleged spy scandal.

Huang has issued a statement admitting making “serious mistakes” in his personal life – a nod to his previous admission of cheating on his wife, allegedly with a suspected Chinese spy.

double quotation markI created problems for the Board that I deeply regret. I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board’s independent investigation.

But Huang also indicated he would be happy to return to his role, saying:

double quotation markSince my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO. Many continue to reach out to me directly as the company navigates complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics. NVIDIA is a once-in-a-generation company.

If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.

Here’s the full story:

Huang, and Nvidia’s top lawyer, have agreed to testify to Congressional committees next month.

Stock markets have fallen across Europe and in New York, ahead of Nvidia’s results after today’s closing Wall Street bell.

The tech-focused Nasdaq led the fallers, down 1.6%.

In London, the FTSE 100 posted its biggest one-day fall since March, falling by 1.76%.

Investors are eager to hear tonight whether Nvidia is sticking to its financial guidance, following the scandal which forced out CEO Jensen Huang last week.

The company has already announced the creation of a National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee, to keep tabs on its operations.

Two US departments have confirmed that Megaspeed is being investigated for violating US export controls by helping to ship tech giant Nvidia’s chips to China.

In a joint statement, the US Department of Justice and Department of Commerce said they had been investigating Singapore-based firm Megaspeed since 2024.

China has hit back after the US closed a loophole which allowed Chinese firms to access Nvidia-powered data centres in third-party countries.

China’s foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said Beijing would take “necessary measures” to safeguard its own interests, saying:

double quotation mark“The US has repeatedly overstretched the concept of national security, abused export controls and even interfered in China’s normal trade and technological cooperation with other countries, unjustifiably suppressing the development of China’s high-tech industries.”

FinanceTab.title: United Airlines says ‘widespread’ system outage resolved
FinanceTab.text:
United ⁠Airlines said on ⁠Monday ⁠that it had resolved ⁠a widespread system ⁠outage, just three days after the Federal ⁠Aviation Administration issued a rare nationwide ground stop on all US flights.

“We have resolved a technology issue that delayed flight departures. While some flights were delayed, there was no impact on flights in progress, or on United Express flights,” Chicago-based United said in a statement. “There is no indication that this was a cybersecurity-related issue.”

According to an internal memo from ​United’s pilots’ ‌union seen ‌by Reuters, a company-wide ‌web-based outage had affected multiple applications used by pilots, including crew communications. It said United was unable to provide final ‌aircraft weights for departing flights and advised pilots to ​follow airport station guidance on whether to leave their gates.

Before every departure, pilots use performance software, often on a cockpit tablet, to check that the aircraft can safely take off under current weather and runway conditions. The preflight calculations include the aircraft’s weight along with information about the fuel, baggage, cargo and passengers the plane is carrying.

Sean Duffy, the US transportation secretary, said in an interview on Monday night that he did not know what caused the one-and-a-half-hour outage. “This is not ‌an FAA [Federal Aviation Administration] system-wide problem,” Duffy said on Fox News’s Hannity.

The United computer issue is just the latest high-profile technology meltdown to affect Americans in the last few days. On Friday, ageing equipment led to a temporary grounding of all commercial airplanes in the US for more than four hours, sparking travel chaos as thousands of flights were delayed or canceled.

Airlines have experienced similar disruptions before. ‌In August 2025, United temporarily grounded flights after a problem with its Unimatic system, which supplies flight information to systems used to calculate aircraft weight and balance. It was not immediately clear whether Monday’s outage ​involved United’s Unimatic system.

The Trump administration said the rare ground stop stemmed from a fiber upgrade during routine maintenance that led to data flooding, which crashed a critical communication system.

And earlier on Monday, customers reported service outages and difficulty accessing their online accounts at several major US banks and the money transfer service Zelle after a technical issue at JPMorgan Chase caused ripple effects throughout the financial system.

It also comes after a major outage by Microsoft that began on Thursday and lasted into the next day, which crippled a host of services including Outlook, Teams and AI assistant Copilot. The outage had serious repercussions for millions of people and organizations all over the world, including schools, hospitals, businesses, courts, banks, prisons, police forces and governments.

FinanceTab.title: Americans relying on heating oil brace for harsh winter: ‘We’re often cold in our own home’
FinanceTab.text:
Millions of homeowners in the US will pay hundreds of dollars more this winter to heat their homes as rising energy prices have pushed up the price of heating oil.

The US Energy Information Administration projects households that use heating oil can expect to pay 21% more this year compared with last winter, with warmer temperatures expected to partly offset price increases.

About 3% of US households rely on heating oil as their primary heat source. In the winter of 2023-2024, 4.79m US households used heating oil as their primary heat source, 82% of which were households in the north-east.

A recent report from the National Energy Assistance Directors Association found that overall, heating costs are expected to climb over 7% nationwide, with average heating bills rising 16.9% in the north-east.

Residents in Maine, where the temperatures can reach below 0F in many parts of the state, said they are bracing themselves for a pricey winter.

“My home heating oil costs have doubled this year,” said Heidi Unruh, 61, of Kittery, Maine, where the winter chill comes in December and lasts through the end of March. “They were already impossibly high in Maine before Trump took office, and I will feel serious pain as the Maine weather dives to it’s typical winter chill”

It costs more than $1,500 to fill her 250-gallon tank at home, which has to be refilled every 47 days when the temperatures are low. The increase in costs has forced her to try to cut back on other expenses.

“Between oil prices, tariffs, and rising food and energy prices, it will be an especially difficult winter,” Unruh said. “Mainers everywhere will struggle along with me. To compensate, I grew a lot of my own food this year. I have cut back on unnecessary expenses, and am trying overall to need less.”

Nikki Papadopoulos, who lives in Piscataquis, a county in the central part of the state, said that her family has started to use a wood stove because the cost of propane has also been high. They have also cut back on hot water, trying to use cold water to wash dishes, as the water heater also uses oil.

“We keep our thermostat turned down to the absolute lowest setting available, and honestly, we’re often cold in our own home. We’re wearing layers, sweaters and jackets indoors just to stay warm,” Papadopoulos said. “We’ve cut out pretty much all unnecessary spending. We’re down to the bare essentials.”

Though her husband recently received a pay increase, it’s been nearly eaten up by the higher cost of heating.

“We’re essentially making compromises in our everyday routines just to stretch what’s in the tank,” she added. “We’re taking the hit from every direction.”

Around 50% of households in Maine relied on heating oil in 2024, a reliance that has declined in recent years, though Maine still has the highest proportion of homes using heating oil in the US.

“It’s a necessity. For people in colder regions of America, they need it, it’s what they keep themselves warm with,” said Justin Barnes, a fuel delivery driver in the Bangor, Maine region, who has had to give residents bills that have been much higher compared with recent years. “It seems like these politicians ain’t doing a lick to lower the prices or make our lives easier, which is their responsibility.”

Democrat Troy Jackson, a logger and former state senator, won his election against longtime Republican senator Susan Collins in the recent midterm elections, where Republicans across the country lost their races in what was largely seen as a repudiation against the rising cost of living.

Much of it has been driven by the war in Iran, where the closure of a key oil trading route has led to a prolonged spike in energy prices. Gas prices at the pump have risen over 30% compared with last year. Other oil products, such as diesel and heating oil, have gone up even higher. Recent data showed that heating oil saw a 74.2% increase from September 2025 to September 2026, costing over $6 a gallon on average.

Russia’s export ban on diesel, which is similar to heating oil, amid the country’s war with Ukraine has also affected energy prices, said Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy. In 2025, Russia exported 10% of internationally traded diesel.

The Trump administration has attempted to strike a deal with Russia to export some diesel to the US, but the effort has failed so far.

Bob Carpenter, an electrician in Greenville, Rhode Island, relies on heating oil to heat his home and has had to save up, bracing for the price hikes to refill his home’s oil tank. When his heating oil was delivered last month, it was $1,425 for roughly 240 gallons – about $600 more than he paid in previous years.

The higher cost of heating oil comes atop other bills that have gotten more expensive, including electricity bills. “Two years ago, I thought $250 was expensive. Lately, my bills have averaged around $350 a month, which is starting to feel like the new normal,” Carpenter said.

Carpenter said he’s concerned about the effect higher prices will have on the ability of younger generations, including his children, to save for emergencies.

“When necessities take up more of your budget, there’s less left for an unexpected car repair or a roof that needs replacing,” he added. “What concerns me goes beyond energy. It’s the combined cost of groceries, housing, insurance, and other necessities. Inflation means our money doesn’t stretch as far.”

FinanceTab.title: Several companies are using Trump tariff refunds for corporate bonuses
FinanceTab.text:
Several companies that received refunds for paying Donald Trump’s tariffs have put those funds towards corporate bonuses instead of reimbursing consumers, an investigation from ProPublica has found.

After analyzing securities filings and earnings calls, ProPublica identified at least nine companies who said they are receiving tariff refunds and noted they are directing some of those funds to their leadership.

Stanley Black & Decker, a tool company that makes common household products including vacuums, electric drills and measuring tapes, told its consumers they were forced to raise prices because of Trump’s import fees, ProPublica reported. The company is expected to receive at least $298m in tariff reimbursements and indicated some of it will go to bonuses. Executives at TJ Maxx and Marshalls, discount department stores that are set to receive tariff refunds, also said the same.

A spokesperson for TJ Maxx and Marshalls, which are owned by the same TJX parent company, confirmed ProPublica’s reporting, and said that the company received an aggregate of $331m in refunds for a portion of the tariffs covered in the supreme court ruling. Because of these refunds, the company now has “accrue incremental expenses of $112 million for year-end incentive compensation and discretionary bonuses for eligible associates globally”, the spokesperson said.

“Given that this is an accrual, and we have not reached the end of our current fiscal year, we have not disclosed any breakout beyond this,” the company spokesperson said.

In financial disclosures, Stanley Black & Decker said the refund it received “was partially offset by directly attributable costs for variable incentive compensation”, according to ProPublica. Stanley Black & Decker did not immediately respond to request for comment.

The Trump administration has refunded at least $100bn to companies since August, about 60% of roughly $165bn in tariffs, after the supreme court ruled that Trump’s “liberation day” tariffs were illegal. The court ruled that the tariffs were unlawful because they overstepped his executive authority and should have required congressional approval.

Some companies immediately sued the US government for refunds after the ruling, though Trump signaled that he would “remember” which companies requested reimbursements and praised companies for holding off. The Trump administration has not specified which companies are receiving refunds, despite requests for information, according to ProPublica.

Though many companies said publicly that they had to increase prices because of tariffs, it has largely been unclear what companies are doing with their tariff refunds.

In its analysis, ProPublica found that almost all the companies that have publicly said they plan to use their tariff reimbursements to refund customers are those that deal directly with other businesses, rather than directly consumers. Some companies have remained “vague” about their plans for the reimbursements and have not specified whether those funds will go towards price decreases or holding back on future increases, according to the report.

Research has shown that US consumers have shouldered some of the cost of tariffs, with the New York Federal Reserve estimating that 26% of tariff increases pass through to consumer prices. The Yale Budget Lab estimated that tariffs cost households about $900 annually under current laws.

Tariffs are one of several of Trump’s economic policies that have proven unpopular with voters, reflected in the widespread victories Democrats notched in the November midterms. A year after Trump’s tariffs were announced, a survey from the Pew Research Center found that 63% of Americans felt little or no confidence in his handling of tariffs.

Republican candidates across the country were largely punished for Trump’s tariffs and other White House decisions that have led to greater inflation. In the Associated Press’s November survey of more than 100,000 midterm voters, two-thirds said that Trump’s decisions had fueled inflation, while about half of 2022 midterm voters said the same thing about former president Joe Biden’s policies.

FinanceTab.title: Trump backs calls for reinstatement of Jensen Huang as Nvidia CEO
FinanceTab.text:
Donald Trump has expressed support for the return of Jensen Huang as the chief executive of Nvidia, joining Silicon Valley heavyweights in backing the reinstatement of the AI figurehead.

The US president referred to a tech industry campaign for Huang’s rehabilitation, saying a “big group” of people would like him back.

“I think he learned a big lesson. I guess maybe one lesson is more important than ⁠another, but I would certainly not mind seeing that,” Trump told ​reporters as he left the ‌White House on ‌a trip to Asia. “He could return. There’s a big group of ‌people that would like him to return.”

The comments came as the US government announced a crackdown on companies such as Nvidia selling AI chips and servers to overseas datacentres that in turn are supplying computing power to China and other US adversaries.

Elon Musk, the chief executive of Tesla and SpaceX, and a host of other tech bosses have signed an open letter calling for the reinstatement of Huang.

The reinstatement letter has more than 165,000 signatories and demands that the company’s board members “bring Jensen back while an independent investigation establishes the facts”.

The former Nvidia CEO resigned last Thursday amid reports of extramarital liaisons, including with an alleged Chinese spy, Alice Huang, who is no relation. His resignation ended a 33-year run at the helm of the AI company he co-founded.

Days earlier, Huang had admitted being unfaithful to his wife without specifying who else was involved.

Trump said on Monday: “Nobody’s proven that [Alice Huang] is a spy. She may not be a spy.” Trump has faced questions after it was reported that a US intelligence report about Huang’s relationship with the alleged spy was circulated among senior figures in his administration.

According to the Financial Times, Huang has discussed with people close to him a possible return to the company. One Huang ally told the paper they were putting together ⁠a “war room” of Silicon Valley executives to lobby ​for his return ‌and would try to garner support from ‌the White House. The FT also reported on Monday that Nvidia’s board was not considering reinstating Huang.

One analyst downplayed the prospect of a Huang return, describing the notion of the ex-CEO’s reinstatement as “ridiculous”. Dan Ives, an analyst at Yorkville Ives, said the range of issues facing Huang and Nvidia, from personal conduct to questions over China, made an external candidate or the permanent appointment of the interim CEO – Colette Kress, Nvidia’s chief financial officer – the best option.

“We see no chance Jensen comes back to Nvidia as CEO, and for the company the best path forward is with a new external CEO or Colette,” he said, describing the petition as “noise and distraction”.

The new rule announced by the US government on Monday requires companies in Singapore, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia and Brazil to apply for US export licences for the most advanced chips in an effort to cut down on ⁠them being illegally diverted.

“The rule ‌is designed to ​ensure that ​existing restrictions on access to sensitive American technology cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving datacentres in third countries,” the US Department of Commerce said.

Alice Huang, the alleged Chinese spy, worked as an executive at the Singapore-based Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer. According to reports, Megaspeed is under suspicion of diverting powerful Nvidia chips to China in contravention of US export laws.

Megaspeed said on Sunday it was a “legitimate and lawful business” and that Huang had left the business in late 2025. It added that it complied “with all applicable laws and regulatory regimes, including United States export control requirements and local jurisdiction rules in every market where we operate”.

Nvidia shares closed down 4.1% on Monday, knocking about $160bn (£121bn) off Nvidia’s market capitalisation, lowering it to $3.76tn compared with $4.5tn before the scandal broke.

SportsTab.title: Rassie Erasmus: South Africa head coach banned for six matches following match official comments
SportsTab.text:
South Africa head coach Rassie Erasmus has been banned for six matches by World Rugby over comments he made about match officials in his side's Nations Championship defeat by France last week.

Speaking at a news conference conference in Dublin on Monday before the Springboks' match with Ireland, Erasmus questioned what he perceived as double standards in officiating to the point where he asked: "is that not match-fixing?".

The two-time Rugby World Cup-winning coach was referencing the implementation of new rules surrounding hip-drop and knee-drop tackles, and felt the laws were not being applied correctly.

It comes after Ireland fly-half Sam Prendergast became the first player to be cited for a hip-drop tackle in Ireland's win over Fiji on Saturday, which was not penalised in-play by referee Angus Gardner and television match official [TMO] Mike Adamson.

World Rugby said an independent panel determined that Erasmus' comments "suggest that match officials acted with bias/prejudice or deliberately influenced the outcome of a match".

In response, South Africa Rugby said it has requested a full misconduct hearing and an opportunity for Erasmus to "contextualise his comments and assure the panel that it was not his intention to allege that any match official had acted with ulterior motives".

It is the third time Erasmus has been sanctioned by World Rugby over his comments about match officials.

When he was South Africa's director of rugby, he was suspended for two months by World Rugby after he posted an hour-long video criticising the refereeing in the Springboks' opening Test defeat by the British and Irish Lions in 2021.

World Rugby found the video contained "multiple abusive and insulting comments and attacks on the officials".

In 2022, he received a two-match ban for a series of tweets criticising officials in a defeat by France.

Erasmus' latest ban has been imposed under World Rugby's match official abuse sanction process, which was introduced by the governing body in July.

If the suspension is upheld, Erasmus will miss Saturday's game with Ireland in Dublin (16:40 GMT), next week's finals weekend fixture at Twickenham's Allianz Stadium and the start of his side's Rugby Championship campaign next summer.

Erasmus said that 17 hip-drop or knee-drop tackles had been missed in South Africa's 21-19 defeat in France by match officials. Andrea Piardi was the referee for the Stade de France fixture, while Matteo Liperini was the TMO.

Erasmus added that if TMOs were not intervening for reviews to limit the number of interruptions during a match then it was "manipulation", before he added that his comments were "not an accusation".

"I'm saying if he didn't see it, it must be a technology problem. If he saw it and decided not to act on it, is that not match-fixing?" Erasmus added.

"If the TMO didn't see it, maybe then technology must be better. If he saw it and he ignored it, what does that boil down to? Manipulation of the game or the result or injured players getting injured.

"So all I'm asking, don't take TMOs out and discourage them to get involved. Then the wrong team will win and players will get injured. That's all I'm saying."

In a statement on Tuesday, World Rugby said an independent panel determined that Erasmus' comments had met "the threshold for serious misconduct".

World Rugby confirmed the ban will stop Erasmus having any match day involvement for six matches, which includes coaching, direct or indirect contact with the team management or players on match days, entering the stadium, coaches' box, playing enclosure or technical area.

"The panel determined that the comments suggest that match officials acted with bias/prejudice or deliberately influenced the outcome of a match, and when the conduct is considered as a whole a reasonable person would conclude that the conduct constituted an unacceptable attack on the credibility and competence of the match officials," its statement said.

"In respect to the sanction, the panel determined that the conduct clearly amounts to disrespecting the authority of the match officials by impugning their integrity.

"Therefore, the panel reviewed a number of elements of the commentary including the timing and reach of the statements, combined with the allegations of bias or bad faith, and found that the comments attracted a six-match automatic suspension."

This is the third time in five years Erasmus has been banned for comments about referees, all of them coming after a Springboks loss.

In 2018, he picked South African rugby up off the floor and has won two World Cups to establish himself as one of the greatest coaches of all time.

To his rugby public - the people who really matter in Erasmus' eyes - he will forever be a hero in his homeland.

But outside South Africa his propensity to harangue officials after a rare defeat will tarnish his reputation in the eyes of many.

SportsTab.title: FA want to host Nations League finals in England
SportsTab.text:
England could host the Nations League finals this season after Football Association officials registered their interest.

The semi-final and finals of the competition, due to take place in June, are held in one country.

As well as England, it is understood that Spain and France have also contacted Uefa to register their interest in hosting the final four games, including the bronze medal match, which will run between 9-13 June.

The FA, it is understood, is still discussing potential venues with some doubt over whether Wembley would be available. The only publicly announced Wembley events in June are two concerts by singer Sam Fender, although these are for after the Nations League.

Since the tournament began in 2019, England have never held the finals, with Portugal, Italy, Netherlands and Germany the hosts to date.

Generally, only nations who reach the last four of the Nations League are considered to host the latter stages.

Thomas Tuchel's team will be seeded in Friday's draw for the quarter-finals following their euphoric 3-2 victory over Spain in Madrid, which secured top place in the group.

They could face Belgium, Netherlands, Denmark or Norway in March in the next round before June's finals.

If the FA's bid is successful, it will provide the governing body with an opportunity to host a mini-tournament before Euro 2028, which will be held in England, Scotland, Wales and the Republic of Ireland.

SportsTab.title: Tiger Woods set for competitive golf return in December's Hero World Challenge
SportsTab.text:
Tiger Woods is set to return to competitive golf in December for the first time in more than two years.

Woods, 50, has not played in a traditional ranking event since the 2024 Open Championship at Royal Troon amid a series of off-course issues.

The 15-time major champion has endured a challenging few years with a number of injuries and turmoil in his personal life.

Woods will host next month's Hero World Challenge - an event which is part of the PGA Tour schedule but does not carry FedEx Cup points - and has been announced as part of the 20-player field.

The American is one of three exemptions for the tournament in the Bahamas along with compatriots Rickie Fowler and Gary Woodland.

Speaking to SiriusXM PGA Tour Radio in a video posted last week, Woods said: "I'm feeling better, no doubt about that.

"I've been training quite a bit. I will be at Hero either way, so I'll see you there."

Woods' long-awaited return comes after he accepted a five-year driving ban in September following a plea agreement in his reckless driving case.

In March, Woods had been arrested and charged with driving under the influence after clipping a truck and rolling his car in Florida.

Woods was also found with two white pills in his pocket, which were identified as hydrocodone - an opioid used to treat pain.

He subsequently stepped away from golf to seek treatment in what was described by his attorney as an "intensive, highly individualised and medically integrated programme".

Woods has endured a succession of debilitating injuries, including multiple back surgeries, serious fractures to his right leg following a car crash in 2021 and a ruptured Achilles tendon in 2025.

Woods also suffered the death of his mother, Kultida, in February 2025, while his girlfriend Vanessa Trump was diagnosed with breast cancer earlier this year.

Trump, the former daughter-in-law of US President Donald Trump, said last month that she is now cancer free.

Every report we had since Tiger Woods resurfaced into public life has told us he is looking good and looking fit. Going into the new year he will be taking part in his own indoor golf league, the TGL, so it's not the biggest surprise that he will be at his own tournament in the Bahamas.

This is the fifth time he has come back from a long-term absence from the game at this event. It is one that means an awful lot to him. It is involved with his charitable foundation and it's his tournament, so no surprise this is the one he has chosen to come back at.

The TGL in the new year, that's the indoor simulator run by his company in conjunction with Rory McIlroy. He did compete last year and cut a pretty pathetic figure by the standards of someone who has won 15 major titles. We could see him play before that at the PNC event. That's the parent and child event where he would presumably play with his son Charlie.

He is trying to line himself up to play at least the majors next year. They mean an awful lot to him.

We know how much the Masters means to him, but also think about where the US Open is going to be played, at Pebble Beach, and that's where he won the US Open in 2000 by 15 shots.

The Open Championship at St Andrews where he has won two of his three Open titles. These would be events he would certainly want to be at.

SportsTab.title: Peter Storey: Former Arsenal and England midfielder dies aged 81
SportsTab.text:
Former Arsenal and England midfielder Peter Storey has died at the age of 81.

Storey made 501 appearances in all competitions for the Gunners between 1965 and 1977, scoring 17 goals.

He was part of the Double-winning Arsenal team which secured the First Division title and FA Cup in 1970-71 under manager Bertie Mee.

"Everyone at Arsenal is deeply saddened by the passing of double winner Peter Storey," Arsenal said in a statement.

"All our thoughts are with his family and loved ones at this incredibly sad time.

"We will pay our respects to Peter at our forthcoming home match against Borussia Dortmund."

Surrey-born Storey joined Arsenal as an apprentice in 1961 and made his first-team debut against Leicester City in 1965, initially starting his career at right-back before being moved into midfield.

He is currently eighth on Arsenal's list of all-time appearance holders and was capped 19 times by England, although he did not feature in a major tournament for the Three Lions.

Storey collected runners-up medals with Arsenal in the League Cup in 1967-68 and 1968-69 and in the FA Cup in 1971-72.

He joined Second Division Fulham on a free transfer in March 1977 and made 19 appearances for the Cottagers before his contract was terminated later that year and he retired.

However, Storey had something of a troubled life after his retirement from professional football.

He was convicted of running a brothel - for which he received a suspended prison sentence in 1979 - and was later jailed for three years for his involvement in a counterfeiting operation, then served another prison sentence in 1990 for attempting to smuggle pornographic videos into Britain.

SportsTab.title: England v New Zealand: Seb Atkinson 'ticking off wishes and dreams' as All Blacks loom
SportsTab.text:
England centre Seb Atkinson says he is living a childhood dream as he prepares to face New Zealand in Twickenham on Saturday.

The Gloucester pivot has recovered from a hip knock and is set to return to the starting XV at number 12 for the visit of the wounded All Blacks.

For Atkinson, this weekend's game comes a fortnight after he made his first Allianz Stadium appearance with England in the 45-22 thumping of Australia.

"It's sort of ticking off wishes and dreams that you have as a young aspiring rugby player," Atkinson told BBC Sport.

"Watching [England against New Zealand in 2012] when Manu [Tuilagi] scored that try and set up that try, the big performance in the semi-final of the World Cup a few years ago [in 2019].

"And obviously I was frustrated to not be available last year when the team put in a good performance.

"So a lot of things spring to mind and to be able to be out there and show what I can do on that stage will be really exciting for me personally."

New Zealand - beaten 33-19 by England on the same stage last November - will recall several big-name players this weekend.

They are looking to make amends for a shock defeat by Wales in Cardiff, with Atkinson set to line up against the heralded Jordie Barrett in midfield.

Atkinson has observed and admired Barrett at his best, but he is determined to be his own man.

"I love rugby and I love watching rugby and I love watching the likes of Jordie and [South Africa World Cup winner] Damian de Allende and try and take bits from their game," Atkinson said.

"But I know that fundamentally for me to get better as a player I need to be myself. I can't just replicate other people.

"You're trying to take away what they're good at - but also show what you're good at too."

New Zealand head coach Dave Rennie said his group would "poke each other in the chest" at the start of this week as they pick the bones out of a chastening first loss to Wales in 73 years.

Rennie said the All Blacks "let the country down" against the Welsh, but with an expected 500 caps of experience to come into the New Zealand matchday squad, England senior coach Richard Wigglesworth says the home side are preparing for the highest standard of opposition regardless of what happened in Cardiff.

"It changes nothing," Wigglesworth said.

"We get a different team. It is a massive challenge for us. England against New Zealand is an historic game. We just want to bring the best of us and give it a good rip."

SportsTab.title: International Swimming League: Adam Ramsay-Peaty named for All-Star Match
SportsTab.text:
Adam Ramsay-Peaty will headline the International Swimming League's comeback All-Star Match, as organisers vowed not to "overstretch" after past financial issues.

The ISL, formed in 2019 as a fast-paced, franchise-based league, has not taken place since 2021 because of the war in Ukraine and its impact on the league's backer, Ukrainian businessman Konstantin Grigorishin.

As a result, prize money totalling about $7m (£5.2m) went unpaid to more than 300 swimmers - who did not include Ramsay-Peaty - from its last season, but in July the ISL announced it had set up a payment schedule to repay the amounts owed.

On 19 December, the ISL will return with the All-Star Match at London's Aquatics Centre, with Great Britain's three-time Olympic champion Ramsay-Peaty and South African Pieter Coetze the first swimmers named on the Commonwealth team.

"It's very, very exciting and it's one hit before Christmas, which is something we're always looking for and racing some of the best athletes in the world, which keeps me on my toes," Peaty told BBC Sport.

"I think it's going to be a nice rejuvenation, and just being part of that, I think it's incredibly important that we support that as athletes. For us, making sure that it does well is very important.

"You need people with known names, but also high performers in the sport as well for it to be successful."

The All-Star Match will bring the world's best swimmers to London in four teams - Commonwealth, United States, Europe and Intercontinental.

The format of the competition has had a revamp and will involve 96 swimmers competing in 46 races inside two hours.

On Friday, nine-time Olympic champion Caeleb Dressel and Van Mathias were the first swimmers involved to be named, with both set to compete for the United States.

Further team members for the US and Commonwealth teams, as well as the full rosters for the Europe and Intercontinental teams, will be announced in the coming weeks.

It is hoped the All-Star Match will act as a stepping stone to a full return of the league.

"We would love to see the league format return, but we're also learning from previous experiences not to overstretch," said Ben Allen, commissioner of the ISL, in an interview with BBC Sport.

"I think one of the things which is very important for me, to avoid some of our legacy issues happening again, is to manage expectations and not to jump or run before we can walk.

"We do have plans for 2027 and beyond."

The ISL was launched in 2019 in a bid to shake up swimming by targeting a new audience and growing the sport, while offering athletes substantial prize money and other incentives.

Fina, the sport's governing body, initially indicated it could ban athletes who took part in the ISL, but it backtracked on the threat following a furious reaction from many elite swimmers, including Ramsay-Peaty.

The ISL lasted three seasons before its fourth, due to be held in 2022, was postponed after Russia's invasion of Ukraine.

It announced its comeback with the All-Star Match in August, promising the "largest prize pool ever offered for a single night of competitive swimming", though it has not disclosed the figure.

However, BBC Sport understands there remains some scepticism about the event among the swimming community given the money still owed.

In addition, Rob Woodhouse, the chief executive of Swimming Australia, told BBC Sport he felt "trust building needs to take place in order to build credibility of the league back".

He added: "However, any paid opportunity for swimmers to compete is always a good thing."

Ramsay-Peaty did not compete in the 2021 season of the ISL, despite being named as captain of the London Roar team, and said of the relaunch: "I think we're going into a new era of this league.

"I think the league deserves a little bit of leeway and a little bit of support from the athletes and hopefully everything can be settled."

League commissioner Allen said the ISL had experienced no resistance or reluctance from swimmers in signing up for the All-Star Match, and added it was "ahead of schedule" in the repayments, which it says are being made in four annual instalments.

The ISL says the decision to pay swimmers back in such a way "reflects a careful balance between honouring the prize money owed and ensuring the ISL's return as a sustainable competition".

While Grigorishin remains the league's principal backer as it returns, Allen said the ISL was looking for additional income.

"We're also taking a step back and looking for commercial partners now." he said.

"We've announced to the whole world that we're back, so moving forward we definitely are going to be working together with other parties to make sure that is a sustainable model."
